Migdal-gad
MIG-dal-GAD
proper noun
A city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, named in the roll of Judah’s inheritance; the name means “tower of Gad” or “tower of fortune,” Gad being an old word for fortune or good luck.

Biblical Definition

Migdal-gad is a city in the lowland of Judah, named once in the roll of Judah’s inheritance: “Zenan, and Hadashah, and Migdalgad” (Jos 15:37). The name means tower of Gad, or tower of fortune — for Gad was an old Semitic word for fortune or good luck, and became the name of a false god of fortune among the nations, whom apostate Israel later worshipped. Isaiah rebukes those who “prepare a table for that troop” (Isa 65:11), where the word rendered troop is this very Gad, the deity of luck. So the name of this little tower-town of Judah carries in it a warning stitched into the very map of the land: even in the inheritance of the LORD there stood a Tower of Fortune, a name testifying how ready the human heart is to trust in luck, fate, and fortune rather than in the living God. The believer is called to purge such idols from his speech and his hope. There is no fortune, no blind luck, no fickle fate ruling the affairs of men; there is only the sovereign, wise, and holy providence of God, who worketh all things after the counsel of His own will. The tower of Gad falls before the throne of the LORD, who alone disposeth the lot and governeth the least event.

Webster 1828 Definition

A lowland city of Judah whose name means “tower of fortune”; a standing rebuke to the trust in luck that Scripture replaces with the providence of God.

MIGDAL-GAD, a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah.

The name means tower of Gad, or tower of fortune.

Gad was an old word for fortune, and the name of a false god of luck.

Isaiah rebukes those who prepared a table for that troop (Gad), the deity of fortune (Isa 65:11).

The name is a warning against trusting luck rather than the providence of God.

Modern Corruption

The name means “tower of fortune”; it directly rebukes the trust in luck, fate, and chance, which Scripture answers with the sovereign providence of God.

expand to see more

The very name Migdal-gad, tower of fortune, names a live and abiding corruption: the trust of the human heart in luck, fate, chance, and fortune. From the Gad of the ancient nations to the horoscopes, lucky charms, and “fingers crossed” of the present day, men have ever set up a Tower of Fortune to worship in the place of God.

Scripture will have none of it. There is no blind luck and no fickle fate; God worketh all things after the counsel of His own will (Eph 1:11), and the lot cast into the lap is wholly disposed of the LORD (Pro 16:33). The believer casts down the tower of Gad and rests in a providence that is personal, wise, holy, and sure. To say “good luck” as if fortune governed is to forget the God who numbers the hairs and rules the fall of the sparrow.
